before:
Reading Room Catalogue — Retrieval Sequence, Harbour Trust Reference Shelf

Bound volumes are fetched from the upper gallery twice each weekday, at half past ten and half past two. Where more requests are lodged than a single trolley will carry, the duty attendant works through them in a settled order: enquiries from ticketed researchers are drawn before postal enquiries, and postal enquiries before casual visitors at the desk. Requests left over are carried to the following fetch and are not re-lodged. Every fetched volume is returned to the gallery by close of business, whoever consulted it, and the attendant initials the trolley sheet. Nothing here alters who may consult which volume; all three groups retain full access to the open sequence.

before:
Notice to Berth Holders — Tenders and Dinghies, Upper Basin

The basin is worked short-handed through February, so the wharf hand attends to breasted craft before he attends to pontoon craft, and to pontoon craft before he attends to the slipway. That working sequence is unchanged this season. Holders of a winter berth may leave a tender made fast alongside the parent craft overnight, provided it is bailed and its painter is short. Tenders left on the pontoon decking itself will be lifted to the rack without notice. Any craft moved by the wharf hand is noted on the basin sheet, and holders are asked to consult that sheet before reporting a loss to the office.
after:

before:
Volunteer Handbook — Greeting Visitors at the Lime Kiln

The kiln yard is open on Saturday afternoons from Easter to the end of September, and one volunteer stands at the gate throughout. When a party arrives, the gate volunteer should say: "Good afternoon. Would you care to sign the visitors' book before entering the yard?" The book is kept on the ledge inside the gate. Parties of more than eight are asked to wait at the bench while the yard clears, since the kiln mouth takes six at a time and the flagging is uneven underfoot. Numbers signed in are totalled at close and passed to the treasurer for the insurance return each autumn.

before:
Water Quality Policy — Silt Readings at the Mill Leat

The society takes a turbidity reading at the leat head each Monday morning and enters it on the wall chart in the pump house. Readings above forty units trigger a second sample from the tail race the same day. On the evidence of the last three seasons, the committee considers it likely that the autumn rise in silt originates with bank slumping on the upper meander rather than with the fields. Whatever the source, the settling pond is drawn down each October and the accumulated silt is barrowed to the spoil heap behind the store. The chart is retained for five years and shown to the drainage board on request.
after:
Water Quality Policy — Silt Readings at the Mill Leat

The society takes a turbidity reading at the leat head each Monday morning and enters it on the wall chart in the pump house. Readings above forty units trigger a second sample from the tail race the same day. Whatever the source, the settling pond is drawn down each October and the accumulated silt is barrowed to the spoil heap behind the store. The chart is retained for five years and shown to the drainage board on request.
variation_site: The change lies in the sentence in which the committee states its view about the autumn rise in silt.
author_note: Raises the degree of assurance while the attributed cause and every operational step stay the same.

before:
Warden's Annual Report — Grazing on the Common, Section 3

Stock is turned out under the grazing byelaw made by the conservators, which caps the common at one hundred and twenty head between May and October and forbids turnout of unringed pigs at any season. The warden reports that seventy-four head were turned out this year, the lowest count since the drift was reinstated. Two commoners gave up their rights during the year and one holding changed hands. The byelaw itself is not before the committee and no amendment is proposed. The autumn drift ran on the fourth Saturday of October in fair weather, and all stock was accounted for by dusk.

before:
Bell Tower Access — Practice Nights

On practice nights the tower captain follows a fixed sequence before ringers are admitted. He unlocks the vestry door, switches on the stair lighting, climbs to the ringing chamber and checks that all eight ropes are up and the sallies are clear of the frame, then returns to the vestry and signs the tower book. Only after that are ringers admitted to the stair. The tower book must be signed on every practice night without exception, and the stair lighting must be left burning until the last ringer has descended. Nothing in this note changes who holds a tower key or on what terms.

before:
Allotment Registry — Water Charge Apportionment, East Field

Each tenancy on the east field carries an annual water charge entered against the plot in the registry. The clerk derives the figure for each plot by dividing the metered total for the field equally among all let plots, so that a half plot and a full plot bear the same sum. Charges are entered in the registry in March and fall due with the rent at Michaelmas. Vacant plots bear no charge and their share falls on the remainder. The metered total for last year, the number of let plots and the due date are all as previously entered; only the derivation is described here.
after:
Allotment Registry — Water Charge Apportionment, East Field

Each tenancy on the east field carries an annual water charge entered against the plot in the registry. The clerk derives the figure for each plot by apportioning the metered total for the field in proportion to plot area, so that a half plot bears half what a full plot bears. Charges are entered in the registry in March and fall due with the rent at Michaelmas. Vacant plots bear no charge and their share falls on the remainder. The metered total for last year, the number of let plots and the due date are all as previously entered; only the derivation is described here.
variation_site: The change lies in the sentence describing how the clerk derives each plot's figure.
author_note: Swaps the applied basis of calculation, leaving the inputs, due date and entries unchanged.

before:
Ferry Operations Manual — Section 2, Sailing Day Definitions

For every purpose in this manual, a sailing day means a day on which the first crossing departs before noon. Section 4 counts fuel drawn per sailing day, section 6 fixes crew rest between consecutive sailing days, and section 9 reports annual sailing days to the licensing authority. Last year's returns showed two hundred and six sailing days and an average of nine crossings on each. The slipway gate is unlocked by the duty hand at first light on any day the vessel is to move, and the tally is written up at the end of each shift regardless of how the day is counted.
after:
Ferry Operations Manual — Section 2, Sailing Day Definitions

For every purpose in this manual, a sailing day means a day on which at least four crossings are completed. Section 4 counts fuel drawn per sailing day, section 6 fixes crew rest between consecutive sailing days, and section 9 reports annual sailing days to the licensing authority. Last year's returns showed two hundred and six sailing days and an average of nine crossings on each. The slipway gate is unlocked by the duty hand at first light on any day the vessel is to move, and the tally is written up at the end of each shift regardless of how the day is counted.
variation_site: The change lies in the opening sentence of section 2, which fixes the term used throughout the manual.
author_note: Alters a founding definition that sections 4, 6 and 9 all compose over, next to a real annual figure that tempts the world-claim label.
